faqs.question: How many days before Ganesh Chaturthi should I send the invitation?
faqs.answer: A week is the practical floor. Ganesh Chaturthi 2026 is Monday 14 September, so send by around Monday 7 September — that gives relatives time to move a shift or book travel, and it lands before the flood of festival forwards starts.

faqs.question: Should the Ganpati invitation card be in Marathi or English?
faqs.answer: Match the language the invitees actually read, not the one that looks most traditional. A practical compromise that works for mixed family groups: the invocation and the closing in Devanagari, and the date, muhurat and address in English numerals so nothing is misread.

faqs.question: Which visarjan date do I print on the card?
faqs.answer: The two anchors you can print without checking anything are Monday 14 September 2026 for sthapana and Friday 25 September 2026 for Anant Chaturdashi visarjan. If your murti leaves on dedh din, that is 15 September 2026; for anything in between, count your household's day-count forward from 14 September.

faqs.question: Is it rude to invite people through a WhatsApp status instead of a personal message?
faqs.answer: For a home Ganpati, yes — a status is a broadcast nobody is obliged to see, and elders in particular will read it as being invited by accident. Use status as a reminder after a direct message, not instead of one.

faqs.question: Can I use the same invitation for a home Ganpati and a society mandal?
faqs.answer: No, because the two say different things. The mandal card announces a public darshan window and needs the mandal's name and the aarti timings; the home card names a family and gives an address you are choosing to share with a specific list.

faqs.question: What should I say if I cannot attend someone's Ganpati?
faqs.answer: Say it early, say it short, and give a reason. Research on invitation refusals found a bare 'no' almost never stands on its own — people cushion it — which is exactly why so many invitees say nothing at all. A one-line reason plus 'will come for darshan later in the week' is enough.

faqs.question: Do I need a separate line for the aarti time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the line most people leave off. The muhurat window tells guests when sthapana happens; the aarti time tells them when to actually turn up. Without it you will get visitors spread across twelve hours.

faqs.question: How do I invite relatives in another city who cannot travel?
faqs.answer: Invite them anyway and give them something to do. Naming a specific aarti they can join on a video call, at a stated time, converts a courtesy invite into an actual appointment; a card with no time in it does not.

faqs.question: What image format works best when the invitation goes on WhatsApp?
faqs.answer: Whatever you use, keep the text large enough to read at thumbnail size and open the card on a phone before you send it. Fine print is the first thing to disappear when an image is resized, and the address is usually set in the smallest type on the card.

faqs.question: Is a free Ganesh Chaturthi invitation maker good enough?
faqs.answer: For producing a good-looking card, generally yes. The limits show up after you send: a downloaded image or PDF is frozen, so a wrong aarti time cannot be corrected in the copies already forwarded, and there is no way to restrict who sees your flat number.

faqs.question: Can I send a Ganpati invitation to non-Hindu friends and colleagues?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is normal in most Indian cities. Keep the invocation, drop any assumption about what they know, and be explicit about what the visit involves and how long it takes — 'darshan and prasad, about twenty minutes' answers the question nobody wants to ask.

faqs.question: How do I handle people who say they are coming and then do not?
faqs.answer: Plan prasad for the confirmed count plus the people who never replied, because silence is not a no. Across the 178 public WhatsApp groups studied at ICWSM 2018, 75% of members sent five messages or fewer over six months — non-response is the group's normal state, not a signal about your invitation.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganpati Invitation Card: What to Write and How to Send It

A Ganpati invitation card carries seven things: an invocation, the host's name, the occasion, the date, the sthapana muhurat, the address and a closing line. For 2026 the date is Monday 14 September, and the Madhyahna Ganesha Puja muhurat in Mumbai runs 11:20 AM to 1:48 PM. Two SubhSandesh numbers set the constraint, and both are platform-wide across all 15 page types the site builds, not Ganesh-specific: 49.6% of the 45,656 recorded views of shared pages happen on a phone, and 96.1% of started pages (3,708 of 3,860) get published and shared. Most Ganpati cards now travel as a WhatsApp image or a link rather than paper, which changes the job: the card must survive forwarding, open on a phone, and stay correct if the aarti slot moves. Below: what belongs on the card, the muhurat by city, and what happens after you send it.

## What is a Ganpati invitation card?

A Ganpati invitation card is a short notice telling guests when and where a household or a mandal has installed its Ganesh idol, and when they may come for darshan, aarti and prasad. It is not a wedding card: no seating, no plus-one, and the guest list is usually open-ended within a family, a building or a street.

That looseness is why the format matters more than the artwork. A wedding invitation is answered; a Ganpati invitation is read and acted on three days later by someone who was forwarded it.

This genre is documented. Alaeddin Banikalef's [analysis of 120 online invitation cards](https://doi.org/10.5539/ijel.v10n5p173) collected from Facebook between March and June 2020 found seven recurring moves, six of them obligatory, beginning with a religious invocation and ending with a closing. A Ganpati card runs that shape with Hindu content in the invocation slot.

## Seven things a Ganpati invitation card has to carry

Each is one line on the card, not a paragraph, top to bottom in this order.

### 1. The invocation

One line of Ganesh salutation at the very top — "श्री गणेशाय नमः" or "Ganpati Bappa Morya". In Banikalef's 120-card corpus the opening move was a religious formula, and it works: it marks the image as a religious invitation rather than a party flyer, which changes how a stranger treats a forward from an unknown number.

### 2. Who is inviting

The household or mandal name, written the way people say it aloud — "The Kulkarni family, B-704" or "Shri Siddhivinayak Mitra Mandal, Building C". A card landing in a 143-member group is read by people who cannot work out the sender from a phone number. Name the host inside the image, not just above it.

### 3. What the occasion is

Say which Ganpati this is and how long the murti stays: "Our 12th Ganpati, dedh din" or "Ganeshotsav 2026, five days". Those three words remove the commonest follow-up question — when is the visarjan — and therefore the message your group will never send.

### 4. The date, written out

Monday, 14 September 2026. Weekday, numeral, month, year. Not "Chaturthi" alone, and not "14/09" — a forwarded card gets opened in October by someone who needs the year. If the murti leaves before Anant Chaturdashi, print the visarjan day too: Friday 25 September 2026.

### 5. The sthapana muhurat

Print the Madhyahna window, because sthapana is prescribed for the midday part of the day. In Mumbai that is 11:20 AM to 1:48 PM. Then print the arrival time you actually want — "Sthapana 11:30 AM, aarti 12:30 PM, prasad from 1:00 PM". A window with no arrival time is what produces a doorbell at 7 PM.

### 6. The address, and how much of it to publish

Flat number, building, landmark, and a maps link. Think about this one before posting to a group: the 178 public WhatsApp groups studied at ICWSM 2018 had a median of 127 members, and your flat number travels with every forward. Going wide? Put the building and landmark on the card; give the flat number in the reply.

### 7. The closing line

"Ganpati Bappa Morya", or "आपली उपस्थिती हवी आहे" — one line telling the reader the card has ended. Closing was one of Banikalef's seven moves, and its absence is why some invitation images read as a crop of something longer.

## The muhurat window to print: 14 September 2026, by city

Ganesh Chaturthi 2026 falls on Monday 14 September. The Chaturthi tithi begins at 07:06 AM on 14 September and ends at 07:44 AM on 15 September. Sthapana belongs in the Madhyahna portion of the day, which is why the printed window is midday rather than sunrise.

It moves by city, and by more than most people assume — 29 minutes between Mumbai and Chennai. These are the [Madhyahna Ganesha Puja windows for 14 September 2026](https://www.drikpanchang.com/festivals/ganesh-chaturthi/ganesh-chaturthi-date-time.html?geoname-id=1275339&year=2026):

| City | Madhyahna Ganesha Puja Muhurat, 14 Sep 2026 |
| --- | --- |
| Mumbai | 11:20 AM – 1:48 PM |
| Pune | 11:16 AM – 1:44 PM |
| New Delhi | 11:02 AM – 1:31 PM |
| Hyderabad | 10:58 AM – 1:25 PM |
| Chennai | 10:51 AM – 1:18 PM |

Two cities, two different moments.

## Where the card actually goes: a group that mostly does not reply

An invitation card is not read the way its designer imagines. It is posted into a group, and it scrolls.

Kiran Garimella and Gareth Tyson collected 454,000 messages from 45,000 users across [178 public WhatsApp groups](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/14989) over six months, averaging 143.3 participants per group. Participation was extremely lopsided: the top 1% of users produced 37% of all messages, and 75% of users sent five messages or fewer in the entire period.

Design the card around that. A group is a broadcast channel with a handful of speakers: the invitation is seen by nearly everyone and answered by almost nobody. Silence is not disinterest — it is what three-quarters of members always do.

The card must also be self-sufficient: whatever you type above the image is scrolled past, and only what is inside it survives the forward.

## Why nobody RSVPs, and what to ask instead

Saying no to an invitation is expensive. In a Discourse Completion Task with 120 participants, Angela Litvinova and Tatiana Larina found a [direct refusal never stood alone](https://rudn.tlcjournal.org/issues/7%281%29-08.html): it was always followed by mitigation, an excuse or an expression of regret, because refusing is a dispreferred act that threatens the face of both people. Silence costs nothing and achieves the same thing.

So stop asking "are you coming?". Ask something with a cheap answer.

Who you invite matters as much. Jelena Smiljanic and Marija Mitrovic Dankulov analysed [four Meetup groups](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0171565) with more than three thousand organised events each, on a platform where every member answers yes or no to every invitation. The networks grew mainly through the big events; the small ones did the work of cohesion, and after a handful of attendances, strengthening existing ties mattered more than meeting new people.

For a Ganpati: the open darshan window widens the circle, the 12:30 aarti with fourteen people deepens it. Print both times and let people pick.

The rule: decide the slot yourself, print it on the card, and ask back only for the one thing you need — a head count for prasad, or a choice between two aarti times. A binary question gets answered; an open RSVP does not.

## Printed card, card-maker image, PDF or a page — what changes

The four formats differ on two things that matter only after sending: correcting a wrong time, and controlling who sees your address.

| Format | Recipient needs | Fix a wrong muhurat after sending | Restrict who sees the address |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Printed card | Nothing | No — reprint and redeliver | No |
| Card-maker JPEG on WhatsApp | Nothing | No — every forwarded copy is frozen | No |
| Card-maker PDF download | A PDF viewer | No — resend the file | No |
| A page at one link | A browser | Yes — the same URL updates for everyone | Yes — 42.1% of SubhSandesh creators password-protect before sharing (1,625 of 3,860, platform-wide, measured 2026-09-08) |

Paper and JPEG are finished the moment they leave your hands. A link is not.

That is the argument for [a Ganesh Chaturthi page the recipient performs themselves](/happy-ganesh-chaturthi), where they offer the durva, kumkum, flowers and modak, the aarti thali circles while Karpur Gauram plays, and they write their own prarthana back, on your photo and your mandap. The same mechanics sit behind the [animated shaadi invitation card](/shaadi-card); the rest are in the [full template gallery](/templates).

## When a page is the wrong choice for a Ganpati invite

A link cannot hand anyone a modak and it cannot stand in for being at your mandap. If the person you are inviting lives four buildings away, walk over.

Paper wins in three cases: an elderly relative who does not open links; a society noticeboard, where the card must be a physical object at eye level; and a mandal's street invitation, read by people walking past rather than holding a phone.

The mobile number cuts both ways. Across all 45,656 recorded views of SubhSandesh pages — platform-wide, across 15 page types, not Ganesh pages — 49.6% happen on a phone, so slightly more than half do not. A card designed only for a phone screen is wrong for half its readers.

One more limit, stated plainly: SubhSandesh has created 3,860 pages since 12 March 2026 across 15 page types, and the Ganesh template is days old with no pages of its own. Every number here describes platform behaviour, not Ganesh behaviour.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

## Sources

- Smiljanic, J. and Mitrovic Dankulov, M., "Associative nature of event participation dynamics: A network theory approach", *PLOS ONE* 12(2): e0171565, published 6 February 2017.
- Banikalef, A. A., "Discourse Analysis of Jordanian Online Wedding Invitation Cards During COVID-19 Pandemic", *International Journal of English Linguistics* 10(5), 14 July 2020.
- Litvinova, A. V. and Larina, T. V., "Mitigation tools and politeness strategies in invitation refusals", *Training, Language and Culture* 7(1), 2023.
- Drik Panchang, "2026 Ganesh Chaturthi date and puja time for Mumbai" — continuously updated, no publication date; retrieved 9 September 2026.

auditReport.honestAssessment: This post cannot rank for `ganesh chaturthi invitation card online free maker`. That SERP is 100% tool pages — Canva, Adobe Express, DesiEvite, CraftyArt, MyNameArt, EasyInvite, InvitationIndia and an exact-match domain — and Google is answering a do-query with software, not an article. No blog post wins that, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. What the post can win is the long tail those tool pages leave completely empty and the answer-engine citation that goes with it: not one of them states the 2026 date, the Madhyahna muhurat, or what a Ganpati card has to contain. An engine asked "what time do I put on a Ganpati invitation card?" has nothing else to cite — this page pairs the per-city muhurat windows for 14 September 2026 with the reason invitations posted to WhatsApp groups go unanswered, from a 178-group ICWSM dataset, and with SubhSandesh's own share rates. Two caveats stated plainly: every first-party number here is platform-wide across 15 page types because the Ganesh template has created zero pages, and journals.plos.org has no batch slot left after this post. Its practical job is to send the reader to the tool the SERP is actually asking for, at /happy-ganesh-chaturthi.
